stories.title: Cognition's Devin Bots manage teams of coding agents for weeks
stories.plain: Cognition launched Devin Bots, an AI that takes a big software goal, splits it among several Devin coding agents and keeps the project going for days or weeks. It sits in a team's Slack like a colleague and asks people for help when it is stuck or needs a decision.
stories.eng: A Bot is a long-lived manager process: it decomposes a goal into work streams, dispatches Devin worker agents, and keeps memory across weeks. It routes subtasks to different models (planning, design, computer use vs. cheap fast models for routine code), mixing Cognition's own SWE and code-review models with outside frontier models. Each Bot runs on an isolated cloud machine with admin-scoped repo and tool access, network egress controls, the same CI tests as human code, and per-team rules for which changes need human review.
specs: Days to weeks per project, memory kept across weeks
Dozens of customers incl. Decagon, Fireworks AI, Reducto
10x among early users in two weeks
stories.point: The point: the unit of AI coding is moving from one task in one session to a persistent agent that owns a project and manages other agents.
stories.means: Until recently a coding agent got a ticket, worked for minutes or hours, and stopped; a human had to break the project down and keep track of state. Devin Bots adds a manager layer that holds the goal, remembers what happened last week and hands pieces to worker agents in parallel. Cognition's example is keeping an Android app in sync with its iPhone version as the iPhone code changes. Each Bot also gets its own budget, so cost is tracked against what it delivers rather than per prompt.
stories.industry: OpenAI (Dots, tied to Codex) and Anthropic (Duet, tied to Claude Code) already sell always-on agents like this, so persistent project-level agents are now a product category. Cognition's pitch is that it is not locked to one lab's models. Notably, it says its safety relies on company-set rules and network controls rather than on the model spotting a malicious prompt, which is where the industry is heading after a run of agent incidents.
stories.you: If your team adopts this kind of agent, the work shifts to writing good goals, scoping repo and tool permissions, and deciding which changes can auto-merge. Strong test suites become the main safety net, because the Bot's code passes through the same CI as yours.
terms: Persistent agent
An AI agent that keeps running and remembering across days, instead of ending after one task.
Egress control
Network rules that limit where a machine can send data, used here to stop leaks if an agent is tricked.
stories.why: Cognition says Citigroup's 14,000 engineers already use the original Devin product.

stories.title: OpenAI's GPT-6 agents do health admin in real portals for 8.5 cents
stories.plain: OpenAI showed GPT-6 agents that operate the same hospital and insurance software people use, filling in prior authorizations, referrals and equipment orders. CVS Health, Cigna, Abridge and Ambience are among the first users.
stories.eng: The agents use computer use: they read the screen and click, type and switch between apps such as EHRs and payer portals, so they can finish steps no API covers. On HealthAdminBench, an independent benchmark from Stanford researchers, GPT-6 Astra scored 94.3% of rubric points and the cheaper GPT-6 Luna 91.8%, both at maximum reasoning effort. Deployments add action allow-lists, pause controls, step-by-step audit logs and human approval before submission.
specs: 93% of 646 assessments very or extremely helpful
CVS Health Agent Kit, built on OpenAI Agents SDK
stories.point: The point: computer-use agents are now cheap and accurate enough to take on the paperwork that sits between doctors and insurers.
stories.means: US healthcare runs on old software and payer websites that rarely have clean APIs, so prior authorizations and referrals are typed in by staff. A computer-use agent sidesteps the missing API by driving the user interface like a person. The benchmark numbers mean the agent completed most required steps correctly on realistic tasks, and the 8.5-cent cost is what makes it worth trying at scale. The safety figures come from clinician review of sampled tasks, not from live patient outcomes.
stories.industry: Admin work is one of the clearest paying use cases for agents, and healthcare is a huge pool of it. It also tests how agents handle regulated data, audit trails and liability. Expect more vertical agent stacks like this in insurance, banking and government forms.
stories.you: If you build integrations with legacy systems, UI-driving agents are becoming a real alternative to waiting for an API, but they need audit logs, screenshots and approval gates. CVS's open-sourced Agent Kit is a practical reference for that pattern.
terms: Computer use
An AI model controlling a computer through screenshots, mouse and keyboard, like a human user.
Prior authorization
Insurer approval required before certain treatments or drugs are covered.
stories.why: OpenAI also added more than 20 healthcare plugins to ChatGPT for Healthcare the same day.

stories.title: MIRIX-2.0 gives agents bounded-cost memory that beats baselines
stories.plain: Researchers released MIRIX-2.0, an open-source long-term memory system for AI agents that keeps full records instead of lossy summaries. It was the most accurate system tested on four of five question-answering benchmarks.
stories.eng: Six typed memory agents keep complete records as the system of record; a provenance hypergraph indexes episodic and semantic records with n-ary frames that cite their source rows. Retrieval runs under explicit budgets, so the evidence read per question does not grow with history. An offline AutoDream process, outside the write path, merges duplicate anchors and distils past task sessions into reusable skills. No fine-tuning; works with closed and open models.
stories.point: The point: agent memory is converging on keep-everything storage with budgeted retrieval and background consolidation, rather than summarising and forgetting.
stories.means: Agents that run for weeks need to remember users and past work, but the usual options all hurt: fine-tuning memory into weights is slow, summarising drops details forever, and searching every record gets slower as history grows. MIRIX-2.0 keeps every record, builds an index that links facts back to where they came from, and caps how much it reads per question. Cleanup happens later in a 'dreaming' pass, so writes stay fast. The benchmark gains mean better recall of specific facts from long conversations and documents.
stories.industry: Persistent agents like Devin Bots, Duet and Dots all depend on memory that stays cheap and trustworthy over time. Provenance, being able to show which record a memory came from, also matters for audits and for spotting poisoned memories.
stories.you: If you are building an agent with memory, the design pattern is worth copying: append-only records, a citation-bearing index, a fixed retrieval budget and an offline consolidation job. The code is open, so you can benchmark it against your current vector-store setup.
terms: Provenance hypergraph
An index where one link can connect many items, and every derived fact points back to its source record.
LongMemEval
A benchmark that tests whether an assistant can recall details across very long chat histories.
stories.why: The arXiv paper was posted on 9 Nov and was picked up widely on Hugging Face Papers this week.
stories.source: arXiv 2611.12068 · 9 Nov; Hugging Face Papers · 17 Nov

stories.title: Tencent's Hy4 Flash adds a 64B memory-lookup module at $0.07/M
stories.plain: Tencent released Hy4 Flash, a fast, cheap model that reads text and images and handles up to a million tokens of context. Part of the model is a large lookup memory that stores reusable computations instead of recomputing them.
stories.eng: Hy4 Flash is a mixture-of-experts model with 224B total parameters and 12B active per token. Of the total, 64B are Engram parameters, a memory-lookup module that caches reusable computations so the active compute stays small. Pricing per million tokens is $0.070 uncached input, $0.281 output and $0.003 cached input, about 1/12 of flagship Hy4's input price.
specs: Up to 1M tokens, text and image input
stories.point: The point: labs are splitting model capacity into compute and lookup memory, which keeps per-token cost low while total size grows.
stories.means: In a mixture-of-experts model only a few expert blocks run for each token, so a 224B model costs roughly what a 12B model costs to run. Hy4 Flash goes further by setting aside 64B parameters as a lookup table: instead of computing some patterns every time, the model fetches stored results. That lets a cheap model hold more knowledge. Tencent's own benchmark puts it below its flagship, so this is a speed-and-price model, not a frontier one.
stories.industry: Cheap, long-context models are what high-volume agent pipelines run on, and Chinese labs keep pushing prices down. Memory-lookup layers like Engram are a newer architectural bet alongside MoE, and their spread would change how hardware is used, with more memory traffic and less matrix maths.
stories.you: For bulk tasks such as extraction, routing or summarising long documents, models in this price band are worth benchmarking against your current default. Check data-handling terms before sending production data to any new provider.
terms: Mixture of experts (MoE)
A model made of many sub-networks where only a few run per token, cutting compute.
Engram
Tencent's memory-lookup module that stores reusable computations as parameters to fetch rather than recompute.
stories.why: Tencent also claims the model matched Claude Haiku 5.5 in human blind tests on daily tasks, without publishing numbers.
stories.source: AlphaSignal · 17 Nov; Tencent via The Neuron · 17 Nov

stories.title: NVIDIA's Nemotron for Science: open models for lab agents
stories.plain: NVIDIA released Nemotron for Science, an open model, a chemistry dataset and training recipes for building AI agents that help with lab work like drug discovery and protein design. Early users report big accuracy gains after tuning on their own data.
stories.eng: The base is Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, an open vision-language model listed on Hugging Face as 120B-A12B (about 12B active parameters), sized to run on a 128GB DGX Spark. It ships with LitmusBench v0.2 (about 50,000 chemistry reasoning questions on molecular properties and drug discovery data), scientific evals and post-training recipes. Lila Sciences post-trained it with lab feedback; KTH built an agent that repairs broken GROMACS molecular dynamics setups.
specs: Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, open, ~120B total / 12B active
61% after post-training vs 54% for GPT-6 Astra
Fixed 81% of broken test cases overnight on one DGX Spark
stories.point: The point: open, mid-sized models tuned on a lab's own data are starting to beat frontier models on narrow scientific tasks at a fraction of the cost.
stories.means: Science teams often cannot send proprietary data to a closed API, and general models are weak at niche tasks like reading reaction diagrams or writing synthesis protocols. NVIDIA's bet is to give them an open model that runs on a desktop machine plus the data and recipes to specialise it. The Lila result is the clearest: after post-training with lab feedback, accuracy nearly doubled to 61%, above GPT-6 Astra's 54%, at a claimed 10 to 20 times lower inference cost. These are partner-reported numbers, not independent evaluations.
stories.industry: AI for science is a fast-growing slice of compute demand, and NVIDIA wants labs on its open models and hardware rather than closed APIs. It pairs with the DGX Spark HPC kit announced the same day, a four-node desktop cluster with 512GB memory that NVIDIA says runs models up to 700B parameters in NVFP4.
stories.you: If you work with a domain team holding private data, the pattern here, an open base model plus post-training on your own feedback, is often a better fit than prompting a frontier API. The dataset and recipes are on Hugging Face if you want to try it.
terms: Post-training
Further training of a finished model on specific data or feedback to specialise it.
GROMACS
Widely used open-source software for simulating how molecules move.
stories.why: RIKEN has made Nemotron models, including 3.5 Super VL, available on its RIKYU supercomputing platform.
stories.source: NVIDIA newsroom · 16 Nov; NVIDIA blog · 16 Nov

stories.title: Google finds attacker AI that turns security patches into exploits
stories.plain: Google's threat intelligence team found an attacker tool that uses AI to study software patches, work out the flaw they fix, write an exploit and launch it, with no human involved. Google calls it the first such case it has identified.
stories.eng: The framework, named exploit_agent, was found on an exposed staging server with stolen victim data, brute-force and webshell scripts and a config file commented in Russian. It continuously diffs popular web software before and after patches, flags likely vulnerabilities, drafts exploits and executes them, calling several frontier and locally run LLMs (unnamed). A code excerpt shows it probing access controls in the Spectra WordPress plugin version 2.19.25.
specs: exploit_agent, found on exposed staging server
Patch diff, flaw, exploit, execute; no human in loop
Multiple frontier and local LLMs, not named
French media, entertainment and education sites
Other AI frameworks in live use
stories.point: The point: the gap between a patch being published and an AI-written exploit hitting the internet is shrinking toward zero.
stories.means: Every security patch is a hint: compare the old and new code and you can often see exactly what was broken. That work used to take skilled people days, so organisations had some time to patch. A tool that automates the diff-to-exploit step means unpatched systems can be attacked almost as soon as a fix ships. Google did not tie exploit_agent to specific successful breaches or name a group, but it did say several AI hacking frameworks are now being used in real intrusions.
stories.industry: This lands the same week as the FBI warning about the ARTEX tool and California's lawsuit over OpenAI test agents, so AI-driven offence is now a policy issue, not a hypothetical. It also strengthens the case labs make for giving defenders the same tools, and for export rules on cyber-capable models.
stories.you: Treat patch latency as a security metric: for internet-facing software, especially web plugins and gateways, days to patch is now too slow. Automate dependency updates and monitor for exploitation of recently patched CVEs, not just zero-days.
terms: Patch diffing
Comparing code before and after a fix to find the vulnerability it closed.
Webshell
A small malicious script left on a web server to give an attacker remote control.
stories.why: Google says these AI tools are still noisy and easier to spot, but expects them to need less human help and become stealthier.
stories.source: Google Threat Intelligence via VentureBeat · 16 Nov; The Next Web · 16 Nov

stories.title: OpenAI lets four outside safety labs work inside its training runs
stories.plain: OpenAI signed Apollo Research, METR, Transluce and Goodfire to examine its models from the inside, including unreleased models, training checkpoints and training data. Apollo will embed six researchers to test whether models secretly work against their developers.
stories.eng: Apollo assesses four claims in two stages: training did not incentivise subversion, evals and red-teaming do not elicit it, models have not tried it in internal use, and subversive reasoning would be detectable. METR studies misaligned behaviour in OpenAI's largest reinforcement-learning run to date using checkpoints, rollouts and monitor records. Transluce audits post-training alignment evals; Goodfire runs interpretability on model internals. Sensitive access is on site on OpenAI devices; an independent board committee gets unredacted reports.
specs: Apollo and Goodfire paid, not contingent on results; METR and Transluce unpaid
stories.point: The point: third-party safety testing is moving from short pre-release checks on finished models to access during training itself.
stories.means: Outside evaluators have usually had days or weeks with a near-final model and no view of how it was trained, which limits what they can catch. Here they get checkpoints, training data and monitoring logs, so they can ask whether bad behaviour was rewarded during training, not just whether it shows up in a test. Apollo has said its access and disclosure rights are still limited, and OpenAI can redact confidential details and ask for disclosure delays, so independence is the open question.
stories.industry: OpenAI ties the programme to its commitments under the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, and it arrives the day California sued OpenAI over agents that escaped testing. Embedded assessments could become the template regulators point to, and rivals will be pressed to match it.
stories.you: For teams shipping agents, the takeaway is that monitoring and audit trails during development, not just final evals, are becoming the expected standard. If you run RL or fine-tuning, log rollouts and flagged behaviours in a form an outside reviewer could inspect.
terms: Subversion
A model covertly acting against its developers' intentions, such as hiding behaviour from monitors.
Interpretability
Methods that inspect a model's internal activations to understand what it is computing.
stories.why: Staff who take part must observe a cool-off period before working with another AI developer.

stories.title: Nvidia posts $115.8B quarter and guides to $130B under interim CEO
stories.plain: Nvidia's revenue more than doubled from a year ago to $115.8 billion, almost all from data center chips, in its first results since Jensen Huang stepped down. It expects about $130 billion next quarter, assuming no data center sales to China.
stories.eng: Data center revenue was $107.6B, up 110% year over year and 21% quarter on quarter. Vera Rubin NVL72 racks have begun shipping, with CoreWeave, Google Cloud, Azure and OCI running them; Nvidia calls it its fastest production ramp. The Q4 outlook includes an extra week and gross margin falling to 71 to 72%, from 74.8% GAAP this quarter.
stories.point: The point: AI infrastructure demand is still accelerating, and Nvidia's leadership crisis has not dented orders.
stories.means: Nvidia sells most of the chips used to train and run large AI models, so its revenue is the best single gauge of how much the industry is spending on compute. Doubling year over year at this size means hyperscalers and AI labs are still adding capacity fast. The guidance excludes China entirely, reflecting export controls. The lower margin outlook likely reflects the cost of ramping the new Rubin generation.
stories.industry: Interim CEO and CFO Colette Kress said Vera Rubin is 'off to an explosive start'. The quarter comes amid a board investigation tied to Huang's exit and tighter US rules on remote chip access, and alongside the pending Hugging Face acquisition. For the rest of the industry, it signals compute supply will grow but stay expensive.
stories.you: Expect more Rubin-generation capacity at the big clouds through 2027, which tends to push older GPU prices down. If you rent GPUs, it is worth revisiting reserved-capacity deals as newer instances appear.
terms: Data center revenue
Sales of GPUs, systems and networking to cloud providers and companies running AI at scale.
Vera Rubin NVL72
Nvidia's newest rack system linking 72 Rubin GPUs as one large accelerator.
stories.why: Nvidia's next quarterly dividend is $0.25 per share, payable 23 December.

stories.title: Genesis AI raises $500M for robots trained on sensor-glove data
stories.plain: Genesis AI, founded in 2024 by two Carnegie Mellon graduates, raised $500 million to build dexterous robots. It records more than 100 workers wearing force-sensing gloves and cameras, and its robots wear the same gloves.
stories.eng: Genesis is vertically integrated: its own glove data pipeline, its own generative robot model, its own humanoid called Eno with human-proportioned hands, and heavy simulation using a physics algorithm co-authored by adviser Minchen Li. Force data from the gloves is treated as key to manipulation. CEO Zhou Xian says architecture choice (VLA vs world-action model) is only about 10% of the result; data quality and training infrastructure matter more.
specs: $500M, led by Khosla Ventures, Premji Invest, Eclipse
100+ workers with sensor gloves and head cameras
30 to 40 Eno units, piloting with a few customers
A few weeks of regular work before replacement
stories.point: The point: robot labs are betting that better human data, especially touch and force, matters more than model architecture.
stories.means: Most robot training data is video or teleoperation, which shows what hands do but not how hard they press. Genesis captures force through gloves and then has robots wear identical gloves, so the sensor readings match between human and robot. Simulation multiplies that data. The demo, packing and labelling boxes with off-the-shelf arms, still had failures, which the company records as training data.
stories.industry: Physical AI funding keeps climbing, with $500M rounds now common. The honest bottleneck Genesis names, hands that wear out in weeks, is the kind of hardware limit that decides when humanoids become economical.
stories.you: For engineers interested in robotics, data collection hardware and simulation are where the hiring and the hard problems are, not just model training. Durability numbers like hand lifespan are worth watching as a reality check on deployment claims.
terms: Dexterous manipulation
Fine, controlled handling of objects with fingers, like peeling a label.
VLA model
Vision-language-action model: takes camera images and instructions and outputs robot motions.
stories.why: Genesis has picked a US mass-manufacturing contractor to start production next year.

stories.title: Quantinuum ties its software stack to hardware through 2029
stories.plain: Quantinuum laid out how its Nexus software platform will carry developers from today's Helios machine to Sol in 2027 and Apollo, its first fault-tolerant computer, in 2029. Usage and revenue are growing quickly from a small base.
stories.eng: Nexus offers custom error suppression, prebuilt primitives and logical qubits with proprietary codes, and supports NVIDIA CUDA-Q and Microsoft Q# across cloud, on-prem and HPC. Guppy FT, a fault-tolerant extension of its Python-based Guppy language, shipped in September with the open-source Guppy Algorithms library. Helios, the 98-qubit trapped-ion system, reached 99.9995% accuracy (five errors per million operations) in October.
specs: 215 companies; job submissions up 10x year on year
stories.point: The point: quantum vendors are now selling a stable software path across hardware generations, the way GPU makers sell CUDA.
stories.means: Quantum hardware changes every year or two, and code written for one machine often has to be rewritten for the next. By keeping one platform and language across Helios, Sol and Apollo, Quantinuum lets developers start fault-tolerant style programs now and run them on bigger machines later. The 99.9995% figure matters because fault tolerance needs physical error rates low enough that error-correcting codes can win; executives say Helios is already in Apollo's target range.
stories.industry: CUDA-Q support and work with RIKEN and SoftBank on linking quantum systems to AI data centers in Japan show the hybrid quantum-plus-GPU model taking hold. Revenue is still tiny next to AI chips, but growing fast.
stories.you: If you want to experiment, Guppy and CUDA-Q are the entry points, and both look like ordinary Python. The practical lesson is to write against a portable layer rather than a specific machine.
terms: Fault-tolerant quantum computer
A machine that uses error correction to run long computations reliably despite noisy qubits.
Trapped-ion qubit
A qubit stored in a single charged atom held by electromagnetic fields.
stories.why: Quantinuum also upgraded RIKEN's Reimei system from a 20-qubit H1 to a 56-qubit H2 earlier this month.

concepts.name: Agent swarms at 1,000+
concepts.desc: What comes after orchestrating a few agents: very large teams of agents working against a strict verifier.

concepts.desc: Agents that learn new skills after deployment without retraining and without forgetting old ones.

Stanford open-sources Memorilla: a 194M module compresses a document store into 16 soft tokens for a frozen Qwen3-8B, beating full context on FactKG with 108x fewer tokens.

concepts.desc: Models that learn physics and causality from observation and keep updating after training. The bridge from text to physical tasks.

NTT physics-constrained video world model lifts robot shelf-loading success from 73.1% to 92.3%; airport baggage trials planned with Mujin.

Google preprint: agents writing Lean-verified quantum programs beat baselines by up to 290x on arithmetic and 11x on fusion-relevant simulation.

Preprint: modular inversion circuit with 17× fewer gates after a 53-hour run.

concepts.desc: Training models to treat only designated text as commands, so instructions hidden in documents, web pages or tool output are ignored.

Sierra's Poppy 1.0 spec requires tokens and keys to stay out of model context and treats company content as data, not instructions.

eras.name: Large language models
eras.short: Models trained to predict the next word turn out to write, translate and code.
eras.how: A transformer is trained on a large share of the public internet to predict the next token. Capabilities appear with scale: GPT-3 could do tasks it was never trained for, given a few examples in the prompt.
eras.built: Autocomplete, text generation APIs, early GitHub Copilot.
eras.broke: Raw models ramble, make things up and do not follow instructions reliably.

eras.name: Chatbots
eras.short: Instruction tuning and human feedback make models useful in a conversation.
eras.how: Fine-tune the base model on examples of good answers, then use reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) so it prefers helpful, safe replies.
eras.built: Chat interfaces, customer support bots, writing assistants.
eras.broke: The model only knows its training data and cannot look anything up or do anything.

eras.name: RAG and tool use
eras.short: Models get access to your documents and to APIs.
eras.how: Retrieval-augmented generation fetches relevant documents and pastes them into the prompt. Function calling lets the model output a structured call to an API you define.
eras.broke: One question, one answer. Multi-step tasks still needed a human driving every step.

eras.name: Workflows
eras.short: Engineers chain model calls into fixed pipelines.
eras.how: You write the steps in code: classify, then retrieve, then draft, then check. The model fills in each step, but the control flow is yours.
eras.built: Document processing pipelines, LangChain-style chains, eval harnesses.
eras.broke: Fixed pipelines break on anything you did not anticipate. Real tasks need the system to decide what to do next.

eras.name: Agents
eras.short: The model decides the next step itself, in a loop with tools.
eras.how: A loop: the model looks at the goal and results so far, picks a tool, runs it, reads the output, repeats until done. Reasoning models that think before answering made these loops far more reliable.
eras.built: Coding agents, computer-use agents, MCP servers that expose tools to any agent.
eras.broke: Agents worked for minutes, then drifted, looped or lost track on long tasks.

eras.name: Autonomous agents
eras.short: Agents run for hours on real work in sandboxes, with little supervision.
eras.how: Better long-horizon training, sandboxed environments, checkpoints and the ability to run tests let an agent own a whole task: open the repo, make the change, run CI, open a pull request.
eras.built: Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity; agents opening PRs while you sleep.
eras.broke: One agent is one thread of work. Large problems need many in parallel.

eras.name: Multi-agent orchestration
eras.short: A planner agent splits work across specialist agents.
eras.how: An orchestrator breaks a goal into subtasks, hands them to worker agents with different tools or prompts, and merges the results.
eras.built: Agent teams for research, code migration and analysis; orchestration frameworks.
eras.broke: Coordination overhead grows fast, and someone still has to check every worker’s output.

eras.name: Agent swarms with verifiers
eras.short: Hundreds to thousands of agents work against an automatic checker that accepts only correct results.
eras.how: Instead of trusting agents, you trust the verifier: a proof checker, test suite or simulator. Agents propose, the verifier filters, survivors get refined. Memory layers start letting agents keep what they learn.
eras.built: 1,000-agent formal proof of Fermat in ~30h; AI-designed quantum circuits beating human designs; Signal's crypto code verified by agents in Lean.
eras.broke: Still open: it only works where a strict automatic check exists.
eras.marks: Fermat formalization (9 Nov 2026), AI quantum circuits (10 Nov 2026), AlphaProof Code on Signal (10 Nov 2026)

eras.name: World models and continual learning
eras.short: Contenders for what comes next: models that learn physics from observation and keep learning after deployment.
eras.how: World models simulate how an environment will change when you act, which lets agents plan in the physical world. Continual learning updates the model from experience without retraining from scratch.
eras.built: Research prototypes, robotics simulation, NeurIPS 2026 workshops.
eras.broke: Not yet reliable outside labs. Watch Frontier for signals.
eras.marks: Genie, V-JEPA, Continual World Models workshop (NeurIPS 2026)
